knowledge_point.title: Integrating Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments

question.:question/problem:
Use the substitution $u=4 x$. Which integral is obtained?

$$
\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{8}} \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=4 x$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=4.
$$

Transform both bounds:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{\pi}{4}&\Longrightarrow u=\pi\\x=\frac{3 \pi}{8}&\Longrightarrow u=\frac{3 \pi}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{8}} \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\frac{1}{4}\left(\int_{\pi}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}} \sin{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

The transformed integral is

$$
\frac{1}{4}\left(\int_{\pi}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}} \sin{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).
$$

Evaluate exactly.

\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{8}} \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x

You may use $\int \sin{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u=- \cos{\left(u \right)}+C$.

Endpoint values: $\cos{\left(\pi \right)}=-1,\quad \cos{\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2} \right)}=0$.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=4 x$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=4.
$$

Transform both bounds:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{\pi}{4}&\Longrightarrow u=\pi\\x=\frac{3 \pi}{8}&\Longrightarrow u=\frac{3 \pi}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{8}} \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\frac{1}{4}\left(\int_{\pi}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}} \sin{\left(u \right)}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate and evaluate:

$$
\left[- \frac{\cos{\left(u \right)}}{4}\right]_{\pi}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}=\left(0\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4}\right).
$$

The answer is

$$
- \frac{1}{4}.
$$
